answer.evidence: Each of the four steps has a tread band 4-5 rows tall that ends in a 1-row light front-edge line (rows 5, 13, 20, 29). Below each line is a dark riser or shadow band of 2-4 rows (rows 6-8, 14-16, 21-24, 30-31), which gives the front face. The rows alternate tread, light edge line, dark riser, so the stairs read as 3/4-view steps climbing north. Rows 32-47 are flat floor. It has no front face, but it is the ground tile in front of the stairs, not the main body.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a brown wooden-looking stair/cliff patch with horizontal plank bands and a flat tan lower area. About 27% of it is near-flat, against 0% in both references. The lower third is a large flat sand-coloured fill with only sparse dots. The upper part has horizontal stripes of only 2-3 browns and no per-step grain or highlights. It reads as a few bands rather than carved stone steps in a cave cliff. It has 6 visible tones per tile, which is above the grass reference (3) and just under the paving reference (7), but the picture shows less structure and texture than either, so the count overstates its richness. Only 18% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the dark lines lean toward brown material tones, but the dark bands are used as uniform stripes rather than selective shading. Shading is shallow (about 3 steps against 5-6 in the references) and there is no stone-by-stone shading.

answer.evidence: The stairs (rows 0-31) are drawn as four stacked steps. Each step has a tread band of about 4-5 rows that ends in a light front-edge line (rows 5, 13, 20, 29 in the column scans). A dark riser or shadow band of 2-6 rows follows each edge line (rows 6-8, 14-19, 21-24, 30-31). This is the tread-plus-edge-line-plus-shadow pattern of a top surface above a front face, so the stairs read as three-quarter view. Rows 32-47 are flat floor texture in front of the stairs.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate's outlines are tinted dark brown (only 18% of dark edge pixels are neutral), so it avoids the black sticker look. The measured 6 visible tones per tile sit between the grass reference (3) and the paving reference (7), so density alone does not sink it. The problems are structure and texture. 27% near-flat coverage against 0% in both references: the lower beige landing is a large, almost flat fill with only a few speckles. The stair and cliff section is mostly regular horizontal bands with about 4 lightness steps, with no per-stone or per-plank shading and little grain. The whole patch uses only 11 distinct colours, so it reads as flatter and more banded than the Beodeul references, which are shaded one stone or tuft at a time. A careful artist would likely not accept it next to them, and when in doubt the verdict is fail.
